speaker: Doctor
text: Good morning, I am Dr. Agent. I see you have a history of high fever and a seizure accompanied by a generalized nonpruritic rash. To understand the underlying cause, can you tell me exactly how many days have passed since the fever started?

speaker: Patient
text: 9-month-old infant. The patient is brought in due to a generalized nonpruritic rash for 2 days. The rash started on the trunk and spread to the extremities. Five days ago, the patient had a fever of 40.5°C (104.9°F) and experienced a 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The infant was born at term, has no history of serious illness, and her immunizations are up to date. The current medication includes acetaminophen.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Measles (Rubeola). The clinical triad of high fever, a generalized nonpruritic rash spreading from trunk to extremities, and a history of a seizure (likely due to febrile status epilepticus) in an unvaccinated or partially vaccinated infant is highly suggestive of measles. Although immunizations are reported as up-to-date, this presentation is classic for measles, which can occur despite vaccination (though rare). I will confirm the diagnosis with a serum IgM test for measles antibodies and review any available images of the rash for the pathognomonic Koplik spots or characteristic maculopapular pattern.
